content: Flat feet, also known as pes planus, is a condition where the foot lacks a normal arch when standing. Symptoms of Flat Feet Most individuals with flat feet do not experience pain or other issues. However, in some cases, foot pain, ankle pain, or lower leg pain may occur, particularly in children. These symptoms should be evaluated by a healthcare provider. Adults may notice discomfort, such as aching or fatigue in their feet, especially after prolonged standing or engaging in sports. Causes of Flat Feet Flat feet are a common condition. In infants and toddlers, flat feet are normal due to loose connective tissues (tendons) that hold the foot joints together. Additionally, the fat in the foot contributes to the flat appearance. As children grow, these tissues tighten, and an arch typically forms by the age of 2 or 3 years. By adulthood, most individuals develop normal arches. However, in some people, the arch may never form. Factors such as aging, injuries, or illnesses can damage the tendons and lead to flat feet in individuals who previously had normal arches. This type of flat foot may occur on one side only. Rarely, painful flat feet in children may result from a condition called tarsal coalition, where two or more bones in the foot grow or fuse together. Risk Factors Flat feet are particularly common in infants and toddlers. Diagnosis In individuals with flat feet, the instep of the foot touches the ground when standing. A healthcare provider may ask the patient to stand on their toes. If an arch forms during toe-standing, the flat foot is classified as flexible, and no treatment or further evaluation is necessary. If the arch does not form (rigid flat feet) or if there is pain, additional tests may be required, such as: CT scan to examine the bones in the foot MRI scan to assess the tendons in the foot X-ray of the foot When to Seek Medical Care You should contact a healthcare provider if you experience persistent foot pain or if your child complains of foot or lower leg pain. Treatment Options If flat feet are not causing pain or walking difficulties, no treatment is necessary. A child’s feet will grow and develop normally regardless of the use of special shoes, shoe inserts, heel cups, or wedges. Children can walk barefoot, run, jump, or engage in other activities without worsening the condition. For older children and adults, flexible flat feet that are painless and do not interfere with walking do not require further treatment after evaluation by a healthcare provider. If pain is associated with flexible flat feet, the following may help: Off-the-shelf or custom-made orthotics (arch-supporting shoe inserts) Special shoes Rigid or painful flat feet require evaluation by a healthcare provider. Treatment depends on the underlying cause. For tarsal coalition, initial treatment involves rest and possibly a cast. If pain persists, surgery may be necessary. In more severe cases, surgery may involve: Cleaning or repairing the tendon Fusing some of the foot joints into a corrected position Flat feet in older adults can be managed with pain relievers, orthotics, and, in some cases, surgery. Prognosis Most cases of flat feet are painless and do not cause problems or require treatment. Painful flat feet can often be successfully treated without surgery, but surgery may be necessary in some cases to relieve pain. Patients who undergo surgery often report improvements in pain and function. Possible Complications Flat feet rarely cause complications other than pain. Potential complications after surgery include: Failure of the fused bones to heal Persistent foot deformity Infection Loss of ankle movement Persistent pain Prevention Most cases of flat feet are not preventable.
